tagline: The book of the promised land: Israel crosses the Jordan under Joshua, takes hold of Canaan, divides it among the tribes, and renews the covenant with God.
overview:
Joshua is the sixth book of the Bible and the first of what the Hebrew Bible calls the Former Prophets (Joshua, Judges, Samuel, and Kings), the long history of Israel in its land. It takes its name from its main human character, Joshua son of Nun, Moses' assistant and successor. His name in Hebrew, Yehoshua, means the LORD saves. The book opens where Deuteronomy ends: Moses is dead, Israel is camped on the plains of Moab east of the Jordan River, and the promise God made to Abraham centuries earlier, that his descendants would possess the land of Canaan, is about to be tested.

The book falls into three movements. In chapters 1 to 12 Israel crosses the Jordan on dry ground, renews circumcision and the Passover at Gilgal, sees the walls of Jericho fall, suffers defeat at Ai because of one man's theft, and then wins a series of campaigns in the south and north of the land. In chapters 13 to 21 the land is divided among the twelve tribes by lot, with cities of refuge set apart and towns given to the priestly tribe of Levi. In chapters 22 to 24 the eastern tribes go home, and the aged Joshua gathers Israel twice to urge them to stay loyal to the LORD, ending with a covenant renewal at Shechem.

Joshua matters because it tells of God keeping a promise, and it does so honestly. It celebrates that not one of God's good promises failed (21:45), yet it also admits that much land remained unconquered (13:1) and that the people's loyalty was fragile. It is also one of the hardest books in the Bible for modern readers, because it describes war and the destruction of whole cities at God's command. A careful reading neither hides that difficulty nor lets it swallow the rest of the book, which is at bottom about God's faithfulness, Israel's call to holiness, and the surprising welcome of outsiders like Rahab who turn to Israel's God.
author:
The book does not name its author. Jewish tradition, recorded in the Babylonian Talmud, credits Joshua himself with most of it, with the account of his death added by others, and many conservative Christian scholars have held that the book was written by Joshua or by someone close to the events. Some details point to at least some writing after Joshua's lifetime: the repeated phrase to this day (for example 4:9, 5:9, 7:26) describes memorials and names that had lasted for some time, and 15:63 notes that Judah could not drive the Jebusites out of Jerusalem, which David later captured.

Most modern critical scholars follow in some form the proposal of the German scholar Martin Noth (1943) that Deuteronomy through Kings forms a single work, often called the Deuteronomistic History, shaped by writers steeped in the language and theology of Deuteronomy. On this view Joshua drew on older traditions, lists, and stories but received its final form in the late monarchy (around the time of King Josiah in the late seventh century BC) or during the Babylonian exile in the sixth century. Others see a smaller editorial hand working on a much older core. What is clear on every view is the book's close tie to Deuteronomy: it repeatedly measures Joshua and the people by what Moses commanded.
date:
Two questions need to be kept apart: when the events took place and when the book was written. The date of the conquest depends on the date of the exodus. Those who read 1 Kings 6:1 (480 years from the exodus to the fourth year of Solomon) as a straightforward count place the exodus around 1446 BC and the entry into Canaan around 1406 BC. Many others, pointing to Exodus 1:11 (the store city Rameses) and to archaeological evidence for new settlements in the hill country, place the entry in the thirteenth century BC. The Merneptah Stele, an Egyptian victory inscription from about 1208 BC, names a people called Israel already living in Canaan, which sets a latest possible date for Israel's presence there.

The book's composition is dated anywhere from shortly after the events (on the traditional view) to the late seventh or sixth century BC (on the Deuteronomistic History view), with many positions in between. Readers who differ on this still agree that the book presents itself as the story of the generation that entered the land.
setting:
Canaan in the Late Bronze Age (roughly 1550 to 1200 BC) was not a nation but a patchwork of small city-states, each ruled by a local king from a fortified town, often at odds with its neighbors. For much of this period Egypt claimed overlordship of the region. The Amarna letters, clay tablets from the fourteenth century BC found in Egypt, record Canaanite kings writing to Pharaoh, complaining about one another and about disruptive groups called the Habiru. Whether the Habiru have anything to do with the Hebrews is debated, and most scholars think the term described a social class of outsiders rather than an ethnic group.

The book's action centers on the Jordan valley, the central hill country (Jericho, Ai, Bethel, Gibeon, Shechem, and the twin mountains Ebal and Gerizim), and then the southern and northern regions. The religion of Canaan centered on gods such as Baal, the storm and fertility god, and El, the head of the pantheon, known from texts found at Ugarit on the Syrian coast. Its practices included fertility rites and, according to the Old Testament, child sacrifice, which is part of why Israel's law treats the Canaanite way of life as a danger to be removed rather than a culture to be absorbed.

Archaeology has raised real questions for the book. At Jericho (Tell es-Sultan), John Garstang in the 1930s dated a destruction layer to around 1400 BC, Kathleen Kenyon in the 1950s argued that the city was destroyed around 1550 BC and was largely unoccupied in Joshua's time, and later scholars have continued to argue both sides. The site usually identified as Ai (et-Tell) shows no occupation in the Late Bronze Age, which has led some to propose other locations and others to read the story as a later explanation of an old ruin. These debates are live and unresolved.
purpose: Joshua was written to show that the LORD keeps his word. The land promised to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob is given, and the book traces that gift step by step, from the crossing of the Jordan to the lists of tribal boundaries. It also shows how that gift is to be received: by trusting God's word, obeying the law Moses gave, keeping the camp holy, and remaining loyal to the LORD alone. Joshua's farewell speeches press that point on every later reader. For Israelites in later centuries, including those who had lost the land in exile, the book was both a record of God's faithfulness and a warning about what unfaithfulness costs.
story: Joshua is the hinge between the five books of Moses and the history of Israel in the land. Genesis promised the land to Abraham, Exodus told of the escape from Egypt, Leviticus and Numbers followed Israel through the wilderness, and Deuteronomy gave Moses' last words before Israel crossed the Jordan. Joshua fulfills the promise of land, at least in large part. Judges, which follows, shows what happened when the generation after Joshua forgot the LORD, and Samuel and Kings trace the rise of a monarchy and the long decline that ended in exile. The New Testament looks back at Joshua as a real but partial rest: the book of Hebrews argues that if Joshua had given Israel final rest, God would not have spoken of another day (Hebrews 4:8).
christ:
Joshua and Jesus share a name. The Greek form of Yehoshua is Iesous, which is also the Greek form of Jesus' name, and Matthew explains that Jesus is so named “because He will save His people from their sins” (Matthew 1:21). The New Testament does not build an allegory on this, but it does draw a real comparison. Hebrews 4 says that the rest Joshua gave Israel in Canaan was a real but incomplete rest, pointing to a greater Sabbath rest for the people of God that Christ brings.

Other threads run through the book. Rahab, a Canaanite prostitute who trusts Israel's God, appears in Jesus' genealogy (Matthew 1:5) and is praised for her faith in Hebrews 11:31 and for her actions in James 2:25. The promise that God would never leave or forsake Joshua is applied to all believers in Hebrews 13:5. The law about a body hung on a tree, carried out in Joshua 8:29, is the text Paul cites when he says Christ became a curse for us (Galatians 3:13). And the book's picture of God fighting for his people against their enemies is taken up in the New Testament and turned toward a different kind of war, not against flesh and blood but against sin, death, and evil powers. These are connections the later story makes, not hidden codes in Joshua.
reading:
Joshua is historical narrative with long stretches of administrative lists (chapters 13 to 21) and several speeches. The lists of boundaries and towns can feel tedious, but for Israel they were title deeds: evidence that the promise had become specific, with real hills and wells and villages attached to real families. Read them as the book's way of saying that God's promises land on the ground.

Watch for the book's measuring rod: again and again events are said to happen as the LORD commanded Moses. Watch also for its surprises. The Canaanite Rahab is saved, while the Israelite Achan, from the leading tribe of Judah, is destroyed. The line between insider and outsider runs through faith and obedience, not simply through ethnicity.

Two misreadings are common. One uses Joshua as a warrant for violence by modern nations or groups, ignoring that the book describes a unique, limited moment in Israel's history tied to God's judgment on specific peoples, and that the Bible never treats it as a model for ongoing warfare. The other dismisses the book as nothing but a record of ethnic violence, overlooking both its honesty about Israel's own failures and the way its sweeping language (all the land, none survived) sits beside passages that show many Canaanites remaining. Many scholars note that ancient war reports commonly used this kind of sweeping, formulaic language. The ethical questions deserve to be faced directly, and the chapter notes do so.

structure.title: Entering the land
structure.summary: God commissions Joshua, spies are sheltered by Rahab in Jericho, Israel crosses the Jordan on dry ground, sets up memorial stones, and renews circumcision and Passover at Gilgal.

structure.title: Jericho and Ai
structure.summary: The walls of Jericho fall and Rahab's family is spared. Achan's theft brings defeat at Ai until the sin is exposed, after which Ai is taken and the covenant is renewed at Mount Ebal.

structure.title: The campaigns in the south and north
structure.summary: The Gibeonites trick Israel into a treaty, a southern coalition is defeated, northern kings under Jabin of Hazor are defeated, and a list records the kings Israel overcame.

structure.title: Dividing the land
structure.summary: The land is allotted to the tribes east and west of the Jordan, Caleb receives Hebron, the tabernacle is set up at Shiloh, and cities of refuge and Levitical towns are designated.

structure.title: Farewell and covenant
structure.summary: The eastern tribes return home after a dispute over an altar, Joshua gives a farewell charge, and Israel renews its covenant with the LORD at Shechem before Joshua's death and burial.

themes.title: God keeps his promises
themes.body: The land promised to Abraham in Genesis 12 and 15 is given. The book repeatedly ties events back to what God swore to the fathers (1:6, 5:6, 21:43-44), and its climax is the statement that not one of the LORD's good promises had failed (21:45). At the same time the book is honest that the gift was not yet fully received (13:1-7, 15:63, 17:12), which keeps the promise open toward the future.

themes.title: The word of God and obedience
themes.body: Joshua is commanded to keep the Book of the Law in his mouth and meditate on it day and night (1:8), and the book measures success by obedience to what Moses commanded. Victory at Jericho comes through strange obedience rather than military strength, and defeat at Ai comes through one act of disobedience. The book ends with the people choosing to serve the LORD and binding themselves to his law (24:14-27).

themes.title: Holy war and the ban
themes.body: The book's warfare is framed as the LORD's war. God fights for Israel (10:14, 23:3), and some cities are placed under the herem, the ban, meaning they are devoted wholly to God, their people killed and their goods destroyed or given to the sanctuary. This is the book's hardest theme. Readers take it as divine judgment on the sins of Canaan (Genesis 15:16, Deuteronomy 9:5), as a limited and unrepeatable command, and in some cases as hyperbolic war language; many hold these together. The same ban falls on Israel's own Achan when he steals from it.

themes.title: Faith that crosses boundaries
themes.body: Rahab the Canaanite confesses that the LORD is God in heaven above and on earth below (2:11) and is saved with her family, while Achan the Israelite is judged. The Gibeonites, though they deceive Israel, end up living among God's people. The book shows that belonging to God's people rests on turning to God, a theme the New Testament develops at length.

themes.title: Rest and inheritance
themes.body: God promises rest (1:13-15), and the book reports that he gave it (21:44, 23:1). The land is Israel's inheritance, divided by lot so that every tribe and clan receives a share from God's hand. Later Scripture treats this rest as real but provisional, a foretaste of a greater rest still to come (Psalm 95, Hebrews 4).

keyChapters.why: God commissions Joshua after Moses' death with the charge to be strong and courageous and to meditate on the law day and night. It sets the terms for the whole book.
Rahab, a Canaanite prostitute in Jericho, hides the spies and confesses faith in the LORD. She becomes a lasting picture of an outsider brought in by faith.
Israel crosses the Jordan on dry ground as the priests carry the ark, echoing the Red Sea crossing and marking Joshua as Moses' true successor.
The fall of Jericho, won by obedience and worship rather than siege, and the first application of the ban. Central to both the book's faith and its hardest questions.
Achan's hidden theft brings defeat on the whole nation. A sober study of sin, corporate responsibility, and confession.
The summary of fulfillment: the LORD gave Israel the land and rest, and not one of his good promises failed.
The covenant renewal at Shechem, where Joshua calls Israel to choose whom they will serve and declares that he and his house will serve the LORD.
